The Category
Observability tools watch passively and require data access. Governance platforms document policies but don't enforce them. Audit processes sample retrospectively.

GLACIS is different: we're inline (in the hot path), we enforce (not just observe), and we prove (cryptographically, not just logging).

Think of us as the flight recorder for enterprise AI—irrefutable evidence of what happened at the moment of inference.

Why Now
EU AI Act (August 2026), Colorado AI Act (June 2026), and emerging state regulations require organizations to demonstrate AI governance with evidence, not promises. Insurance underwriters are beginning to price AI risk—and they need verifiable signals.

GLACIS provides the infrastructure to meet these requirements.

Estruturação e governança de programas de continuidade, garantindo resiliência operacional e aderência regulatória.

GLACIS is AI Policy Enforcement Infrastructure.
We don't observe AI systems — we enforce governance at runtime and generate cryptographic proof that it actually happened.
When regulators ask "were your safety controls running?", most companies can only offer logs and promises. GLACIS provides tamper-evident receipts: Ed25519 signatures, Merkle tree anchoring, deterministic serialization. Mathematical evidence, not documentation.

Zero-Egress Architecture
GLACIS infrastructure runs at your edge—inside your VPC, your compliance boundary. We enforce policies inline. We only see hashes.

→ No BAA required (we never process PHI)
→ No data processing agreements (we don't touch PII)
→ No new attack surface (sensitive data never leaves your environment)

Enterprise AI teams get the compliance evidence they need without the procurement friction of granting a vendor access to sensitive data.

The Category
Observability tools watch passively and require data access. Governance platforms document policies but don't enforce them. Audit processes sample retrospectively.

GLACIS is different: we're inline (in the hot path), we enforce (not just observe), and we prove (cryptographically, not just logging).

Think of us as the flight recorder for enterprise AI—irrefutable evidence of what happened at the moment of inference.

Why Now
EU AI Act (August 2026), Colorado AI Act (June 2026), and emerging state regulations require organizations to demonstrate AI governance with evidence, not promises. Insurance underwriters are beginning to price AI risk—and they need verifiable signals.

GLACIS provides the infrastructure to meet these requirements.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B sales benchmark.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company — the company a sales operator is targeting.
  • A CANDIDATE company — a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).
  - Require both: (1) the candidate's primary product/service overlaps a core
    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

Examples:
  - HubSpot ↔ a smaller CRM/marketing-automation platform: true.
  - HubSpot ↔ a lead-generation agency using HubSpot for clients: false.
  - Shopify ↔ an online-store/e-commerce platform: true.
  - Shopify ↔ a payment processor with no storefront platform: false.
  - Grab ↔ a ride-hailing marketplace: true.
  - Grab ↔ a traditional car-rental operator with no on-demand marketplace: false.
  - Rippling ↔ a smaller HRIS/payroll platform: true.
  - Rippling ↔ device-security software for mobile workers: false.
  - Brex ↔ a corporate-card and spend-management platform: true.
  - Brex ↔ consumer personal-finance budgeting software: false.
  - OpenAI ↔ a foundation-model/API company: true.
  - OpenAI ↔ a consultancy that implements AI tools for clients: false.
  - Datadog ↔ an application-performance-monitoring and observability platform: true.
  - Datadog ↔ a generic IT consulting firm: false.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ an endpoint-security platform: true.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ a general-purpose IT monitoring tool with no security product: false.
  - Procore ↔ construction project-management software: true.
  - Procore ↔ a construction contractor: false.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ field-service management software for trades businesses: true.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ a plumbing company that uses field-service software: false.
  - Teladoc ↔ a virtual-care/telehealth platform: true.
  - Teladoc ↔ a health-insurance carrier with no telehealth product: false.
  - Veeva ↔ life-sciences CRM or clinical-operations software: true.
  - Veeva ↔ a generic CRM with no life-sciences focus: false.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).

    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.

    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.

RelyX is the first Security Decision Intelligence platform that turns cyber risk into financial clarity — so security teams can defend budgets, justify investments, and speak the language of the board.

Security leaders face a persistent problem: they understand risk deeply, but struggle to communicate its business impact to CFOs, audit committees, and executive teams. The result is underfunded security programmes, poor prioritisation, and decisions made on gut instinct instead of data.

RelyX solves this by quantifying cyber risk in financial terms using proven FAIR methodology, calculating real ROI on every security control, and automatically aligning each investment to the business outcomes that matter most to leadership.

→ Quantifies cyber risk as Annualised Loss Expectancy (ALE) in £/$
→ Calculates ROI, NPV, and cost avoidance for every security control
→ Maps security investments to strategic business priorities automatically
→ Supports 258+ frameworks including ISO 27001, NIST CSF, SOC 2, PCI-DSS, and GDPR
→ Runs Continuous Control Monitoring (CCM) across AWS, Azure, and on-premise environments
→ Generates board-ready reports in minutes — not days
→ Provides a Business Value Score (0–100) that benchmarks your security programme against business outcomes

Who it's for:

RelyX is built for CISOs who are tired of losing budget battles, security teams who want their work recognised as a business enabler, and organisations that need defensible, data-driven risk decisions — not traffic lights and heatmaps.

Whether you're preparing for a board presentation, responding to an audit, or making the case for headcount, RelyX gives you the numbers to back every decision.

The result: Security decisions your board will actually understand.

Estruturação e governança de programas de continuidade, garantindo resiliência operacional e aderência regulatória.

entity.name: Shadow Security
entity.description:
Shadow Security builds security infrastructure that helps organizations identify vulnerabilities, manage responsible disclosure, and strengthen data governance.

Our platform focuses on practical security systems designed for modern digital companies and the evolving regulatory environment in India.

Core components of the platform include:

Shastra — a DPDP data governance runtime that records consent, access, and deletion events to generate verifiable compliance evidence.

Suraksha VDP — a vulnerability disclosure platform that provides organizations with a structured channel to receive, triage, and resolve security vulnerabilities reported by ethical hackers.

Astra — an on-demand security scanner that detects exposed services, maps CVEs, and identifies security misconfigurations across web assets and infrastructure. Organizations receive a security score and a certificate reflecting their current security posture.

Shadow Security aims to strengthen the connection between organizations and the ethical hacking community while helping companies build measurable and provable security practices.

entity.name: RelyX
entity.description:
RelyX is the first Security Decision Intelligence platform that turns cyber risk into financial clarity — so security teams can defend budgets, justify investments, and speak the language of the board.

Security leaders face a persistent problem: they understand risk deeply, but struggle to communicate its business impact to CFOs, audit committees, and executive teams. The result is underfunded security programmes, poor prioritisation, and decisions made on gut instinct instead of data.

RelyX solves this by quantifying cyber risk in financial terms using proven FAIR methodology, calculating real ROI on every security control, and automatically aligning each investment to the business outcomes that matter most to leadership.

What RelyX does:

→ Quantifies cyber risk as Annualised Loss Expectancy (ALE) in £/$
→ Calculates ROI, NPV, and cost avoidance for every security control
→ Maps security investments to strategic business priorities automatically
→ Supports 258+ frameworks including ISO 27001, NIST CSF, SOC 2, PCI-DSS, and GDPR
→ Runs Continuous Control Monitoring (CCM) across AWS, Azure, and on-premise environments
→ Generates board-ready reports in minutes — not days
→ Provides a Business Value Score (0–100) that benchmarks your security programme against business outcomes

Who it's for:

RelyX is built for CISOs who are tired of losing budget battles, security teams who want their work recognised as a business enabler, and organisations that need defensible, data-driven risk decisions — not traffic lights and heatmaps.

Whether you're preparing for a board presentation, responding to an audit, or making the case for headcount, RelyX gives you the numbers to back every decision.

The result: Security decisions your board will actually understand.

entity.name: Graham Healthcare Capital
entity.description:
Headquartered in Nashville, TN, Graham Healthcare Capital (GHCC) provides permanent capital solutions to healthcare service and technology companies that have between $5-$75M in annual revenue and up to $10M in profit. GHCC has a differentiated approach that lies between a private equity buyout firm and a corporate strategic buyer. GHCC retains, backs, and aligns existing leadership and core principles, providing a supportive platform focused on long-term, sustainable growth.

GHCC leaders offer backgrounds and expertise in operations, value creation, and finance. They’ve built companies from the ground up and understand the importance of emphasizing culture, integrity, employee retention, and strategic investment overbuilding companies solely to maximize profitability in the short term.

Since GHCC holds companies indefinitely, our investment strategies are long-term in nature and focus on preserving the company's legacy. Founders continue to participate in the profitability of the company via distributions and typically retain a significant equity position in the company.

GHCC’s alignment strategy includes:
• low-leverage utilization
• no management fees
• no hurdle rates of returns or preferred capital that favors investors

Graham Healthcare Capital is part of the companies we invest in – not a misaligned equity investor or beholden to the competing priorities of a strategic buyer.
Unlike traditional private equity, we employ a low-leverage, buy-and-hold strategy, partnering with ownership teams over a longer-term investment horizon. This strategy allows for decision-making that is best for the company and its management.

entity.name: GLACIS Technologies
entity.description:
GLACIS is AI Policy Enforcement Infrastructure.
We don't observe AI systems — we enforce governance at runtime and generate cryptographic proof that it actually happened.
When regulators ask "were your safety controls running?", most companies can only offer logs and promises. GLACIS provides tamper-evident receipts: Ed25519 signatures, Merkle tree anchoring, deterministic serialization. Mathematical evidence, not documentation.

Zero-Egress Architecture
GLACIS infrastructure runs at your edge—inside your VPC, your compliance boundary. We enforce policies inline. We only see hashes.

→ No BAA required (we never process PHI)
→ No data processing agreements (we don't touch PII)
→ No new attack surface (sensitive data never leaves your environment)

Enterprise AI teams get the compliance evidence they need without the procurement friction of granting a vendor access to sensitive data.

The Category
Observability tools watch passively and require data access. Governance platforms document policies but don't enforce them. Audit processes sample retrospectively.

GLACIS is different: we're inline (in the hot path), we enforce (not just observe), and we prove (cryptographically, not just logging).

Think of us as the flight recorder for enterprise AI—irrefutable evidence of what happened at the moment of inference.

Why Now
EU AI Act (August 2026), Colorado AI Act (June 2026), and emerging state regulations require organizations to demonstrate AI governance with evidence, not promises. Insurance underwriters are beginning to price AI risk—and they need verifiable signals.

GLACIS provides the infrastructure to meet these requirements.

Backed by AI2 Incubator | Seattle, WA

We're hiring Rust engineers and accepting design partners in healthcare and fintech.
→ careers@glacis.io
→ glacis.io

entity.name: GLACIS Technologies
entity.description:
GLACIS is AI Policy Enforcement Infrastructure.
We don't observe AI systems — we enforce governance at runtime and generate cryptographic proof that it actually happened.
When regulators ask "were your safety controls running?", most companies can only offer logs and promises. GLACIS provides tamper-evident receipts: Ed25519 signatures, Merkle tree anchoring, deterministic serialization. Mathematical evidence, not documentation.

Zero-Egress Architecture
GLACIS infrastructure runs at your edge—inside your VPC, your compliance boundary. We enforce policies inline. We only see hashes.

→ No BAA required (we never process PHI)
→ No data processing agreements (we don't touch PII)
→ No new attack surface (sensitive data never leaves your environment)

Enterprise AI teams get the compliance evidence they need without the procurement friction of granting a vendor access to sensitive data.

The Category
Observability tools watch passively and require data access. Governance platforms document policies but don't enforce them. Audit processes sample retrospectively.

GLACIS is different: we're inline (in the hot path), we enforce (not just observe), and we prove (cryptographically, not just logging).

Think of us as the flight recorder for enterprise AI—irrefutable evidence of what happened at the moment of inference.

Why Now
EU AI Act (August 2026), Colorado AI Act (June 2026), and emerging state regulations require organizations to demonstrate AI governance with evidence, not promises. Insurance underwriters are beginning to price AI risk—and they need verifiable signals.

GLACIS provides the infrastructure to meet these requirements.

Backed by AI2 Incubator | Seattle, WA

We're hiring Rust engineers and accepting design partners in healthcare and fintech.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B sales benchmark.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company — the company a sales operator is targeting.
  • A CANDIDATE company — a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).
  - Require both: (1) the candidate's primary product/service overlaps a core
    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

Examples:
  - HubSpot ↔ a smaller CRM/marketing-automation platform: true.
  - HubSpot ↔ a lead-generation agency using HubSpot for clients: false.
  - Shopify ↔ an online-store/e-commerce platform: true.
  - Shopify ↔ a payment processor with no storefront platform: false.
  - Grab ↔ a ride-hailing marketplace: true.
  - Grab ↔ a traditional car-rental operator with no on-demand marketplace: false.
  - Rippling ↔ a smaller HRIS/payroll platform: true.
  - Rippling ↔ device-security software for mobile workers: false.
  - Brex ↔ a corporate-card and spend-management platform: true.
  - Brex ↔ consumer personal-finance budgeting software: false.
  - OpenAI ↔ a foundation-model/API company: true.
  - OpenAI ↔ a consultancy that implements AI tools for clients: false.
  - Datadog ↔ an application-performance-monitoring and observability platform: true.
  - Datadog ↔ a generic IT consulting firm: false.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ an endpoint-security platform: true.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ a general-purpose IT monitoring tool with no security product: false.
  - Procore ↔ construction project-management software: true.
  - Procore ↔ a construction contractor: false.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ field-service management software for trades businesses: true.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ a plumbing company that uses field-service software: false.
  - Teladoc ↔ a virtual-care/telehealth platform: true.
  - Teladoc ↔ a health-insurance carrier with no telehealth product: false.
  - Veeva ↔ life-sciences CRM or clinical-operations software: true.
  - Veeva ↔ a generic CRM with no life-sciences focus: false.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company — the company a sales operator is targeting.
  • A CANDIDATE company — a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).
  - Require both: (1) the candidate's primary product/service overlaps a core
    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

Examples:
  - HubSpot ↔ a smaller CRM/marketing-automation platform: true.
  - HubSpot ↔ a lead-generation agency using HubSpot for clients: false.
  - Shopify ↔ an online-store/e-commerce platform: true.
  - Shopify ↔ a payment processor with no storefront platform: false.
  - Grab ↔ a ride-hailing marketplace: true.
  - Grab ↔ a traditional car-rental operator with no on-demand marketplace: false.
  - Rippling ↔ a smaller HRIS/payroll platform: true.
  - Rippling ↔ device-security software for mobile workers: false.
  - Brex ↔ a corporate-card and spend-management platform: true.
  - Brex ↔ consumer personal-finance budgeting software: false.
  - OpenAI ↔ a foundation-model/API company: true.
  - OpenAI ↔ a consultancy that implements AI tools for clients: false.
  - Datadog ↔ an application-performance-monitoring and observability platform: true.
  - Datadog ↔ a generic IT consulting firm: false.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ an endpoint-security platform: true.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ a general-purpose IT monitoring tool with no security product: false.
  - Procore ↔ construction project-management software: true.
  - Procore ↔ a construction contractor: false.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ field-service management software for trades businesses: true.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ a plumbing company that uses field-service software: false.
  - Teladoc ↔ a virtual-care/telehealth platform: true.
  - Teladoc ↔ a health-insurance carrier with no telehealth product: false.
  - Veeva ↔ life-sciences CRM or clinical-operations software: true.
  - Veeva ↔ a generic CRM with no life-sciences focus: false.

  name: Vanta
  domain: vanta.com
  description: Trust-management and compliance-automation platform for helping companies achieve and maintain security certifications.

  description: At GRC Assure, we redefine the landscape of cybersecurity, offering cutting-edge solutions to safeguard your digital assets.
